set1.q: A 52-year-old man becomes ill over 4 days with a temperature of 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), shaking chills and confusion. He looks toxic, a new loud regurgitant murmur is heard, and painless hemorrhagic macules appear on his soles, which are Janeway lesions (painless, nontender spots). Which form of infective endocarditis fits his course?
opts: Subacute endocarditis is indolent, with lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks or months, slow structural damage and rare metastasis. His 4-day, 40.1 °C, toxic illness is the opposite. Tell: high fever and toxicity within days mean acute; weeks to months of low-grade symptoms mean subacute.

Libman-Sacks disease is not one of the two courses infective endocarditis takes, acute or subacute. His 4-day illness with 40.1 °C fever, shaking chills, toxicity and embolic Janeway lesions is the hectically febrile, rapidly destructive acute form. Tell: an infectious, toxic, embolizing picture names a tempo, acute.

Device endocarditis requires an implanted cardiac device, and none is described. The question asks which course his illness fits, and a 4-day, toxic, 40.1 °C illness with rapid valve damage and skin seeding is acute endocarditis. Tell: device endocarditis names a site; acute and subacute name a tempo.

Correct. Four days of illness with 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), shaking chills, confusion and a toxic appearance fit acute endocarditis: a hectically febrile illness from a virulent, invasive organism, with rapid onset typically over 3-10 days. The new loud murmur reflects rapid valve damage, and Janeway lesions show seeding beyond the heart.

set1.q: A 76-year-old woman had a mechanical mitral valve placed 4 years ago. She has 5 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue, and blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely in her prosthetic valve infection?
opts: Correct. Her mechanical valve was placed 4 years ago, so this is late prosthetic valve endocarditis, which is caused by Streptococcus viridans. The 5-week course of low-grade fever and fatigue also fits, since viridans streptococci are a classic subacute organism; early infection would instead be staphylococcal.

Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus, is the classic EARLY prosthetic valve organism, along with Staphylococcus aureus. Her valve was placed 4 years ago, which makes this late disease from viridans streptococci. Tell: early after surgery means skin staphylococci; years later means viridans.

Candida is the fungal cause of endocarditis and is not the expected organism for late prosthetic valve infection, which is Streptococcus viridans. Tell: a prosthesis infected years after surgery with a smoldering course points to viridans streptococci, not a fungus.

Escherichia coli is not among the listed prosthetic valve organisms or the usual acute or subacute causes. Late prosthetic valve infection, years after surgery, is caused by viridans streptococci. Tell: years after valve surgery, think oral-source streptococci, not a bowel gram-negative rod.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man had his aortic valve replaced 6 weeks ago. He now has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and a new regurgitant murmur, and transesophageal imaging shows a vegetation on the prosthesis. Which organisms are most likely?
opts: Viridans streptococci from the oral cavity cause LATE prosthetic valve endocarditis. At only 6 weeks after valve replacement this is early disease, which is staphylococcal. Tell: early after surgery means skin staphylococci; late after surgery shifts to Streptococcus viridans.

Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract and are a native valve and subacute cause. Nothing in this stem points to a urinary source, and infection 6 weeks after valve surgery is early prosthetic disease from skin staphylococci. Tell: recent valve surgery, not a urinary procedure, is the clue.

The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group from the upper respiratory tract is a subacute, native valve cause, not an early prosthetic valve organism. Tell: a prosthesis infected within weeks of surgery points to skin staphylococci, not to airway gram-negatives.

Correct. A vegetation on an aortic prosthesis placed only 6 weeks ago is early prosthetic valve endocarditis, which is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus, both skin organisms. The recent surgery is the decisive clue.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has a fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). No blood cultures or echocardiogram have been done yet. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Nothing here excludes endocarditis; with no cultures or echocardiogram the workup has barely begun. His three minor criteria make it possible, and blood cultures (three sets from separate sites) and transesophageal echocardiography come next. Tell: ruled out requires evidence against the disease, not missing tests.

Criteria are met: fever above 38 °C, the prosthetic valve as a predisposing heart condition, and conjunctival hemorrhages as an embolic phenomenon are each a minor criterion. Tell: count every minor item from the history and exam, even before cultures or echocardiography are done.

Correct. He has three minor criteria: a predisposing heart condition (prosthetic aortic valve), fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), above 38 °C, and an embolic phenomenon, conjunctival hemorrhage. With no cultures or echocardiogram there is no major criterion, and three minor criteria make endocarditis possible.

Definite needs two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor. He has three minor criteria and no major criterion yet, because cultures and echocardiography have not been done. Tell: three minor criteria stop at possible.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis needs a root canal. She developed hives (urticaria) after amoxicillin years ago and can take pills. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Cephalexin, cefazolin and ceftriaxone should not be used in patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin or ampicillin, and she had hives (urticaria) with amoxicillin. Tell: urticaria removes the cephalosporin options and leaves the macrolides or doxycycline.
ruled out by a stated finding

Amoxicillin caused her hives, so she is penicillin-allergic and the standard oral amoxicillin regimen is out. Her previous endocarditis and a root canal still require prophylaxis. Tell: a penicillin allergy with the ability to take pills moves to azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline.
ruled out by a stated finding

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. For a penicillin-allergic patient with urticaria who can take pills, azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline is used. Tell: clindamycin has been removed from every regimen.

Correct. Previous endocarditis qualifies her, and a root canal manipulates the periapical region of the tooth, so she needs prophylaxis. She can take pills but had urticaria with amoxicillin, which rules out penicillins and cephalexin, leaving azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg (or doxycycline) 30-60 minutes before.

set1.q: A 45-year-old woman has 2 months of fever, weight loss and fatigue. A new murmur with a tumor plop (a low-pitched early diastolic sound) is heard, and three sets of blood cultures drawn before any antibiotics are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein), not a new murmur with a tumor plop. Tell: a heart sound like a tumor plop points to atrial myxoma; girdle aching points to polymyalgia rheumatica.

Lyme disease causes fever and, rarely, myocarditis, but it does not produce a new murmur with a tumor plop. Tell: in the endocarditis differential, the tumor plop belongs to atrial myxoma, a neoplastic mimic.

Correct. Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, classically a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble. Her 2 months of fever and weight loss could suggest endocarditis, but the tumor plop and three negative culture sets drawn before any antibiotics point to this neoplastic mimic.

Subacute endocarditis is usually culture-positive (culture-negative cases are only about 5-17%), yet her three sets drawn before any antibiotics are negative. And a tumor plop is the sound of atrial myxoma. Tell: a plop plus negative cultures favors the tumor over infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 61-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis develops worsening breathlessness, crackles and a new loud regurgitant murmur on day 3 of appropriate antibiotics. Echocardiography shows a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. On day 3 of appropriate antibiotics she has breathlessness, crackles, a new loud regurgitant murmur and a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation: heart failure due to valvular dysfunction, the most common indication for surgery. Cardiothoracic surgery is consulted to evaluate the need for surgery.

Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs. Nothing in her history mentions drug use, and her problem is acute valve failure. Tell: a ruptured chord with heart failure needs a surgical evaluation, not a harm-reduction service.

Palliative care can be part of a multidisciplinary plan, but palliative care alone would leave a surgical problem unaddressed. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery. Tell: a structural valve failure on day 3 calls for cardiothoracic surgery first.

Outpatient follow-up does not fit acute heart failure developing during inpatient antibiotic treatment. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the leading surgical indication, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates her now. Tell: a ruptured chord with crackles is urgent, which rules out an outpatient referral.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man with aortic valve endocarditis develops sharp chest pain and a scratchy friction rub on day 5 of treatment. Imaging shows infection spreading beyond the valve ring. Which process explains the new pericardial findings?
opts: Extension of the abscess into the upper ventricular septum interrupts the conduction system; it does not cause pericardial findings. Tell: sharp chest pain with a friction rub points to pericarditis, which follows extension into the epicardium.
Septic emboli to the coronary arteries

Septic emboli to the coronary arteries do not explain a friction rub, and his imaging shows infection spreading beyond the valve ring. When a perivalvular abscess extends into the epicardium, it causes pericarditis. Tell: a rub localizes the spread to the pericardial surface.

Drug-induced lupus is not the mechanism; imaging shows infection spreading beyond the valve ring, a perivalvular abscess. Its extension into the epicardium causes pericarditis, which explains the sharp chest pain and friction rub. Tell: follow the abscess, not the medications.

Correct. Infection spreading beyond the valve ring is a perivalvular abscess, and when it extends into the epicardium it causes pericarditis, explaining his sharp chest pain and friction rub. Extension into the upper ventricular septum would instead interrupt the conduction system.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 75-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve needs a dental extraction. He had a mild delayed rash (no hives, swelling or anaphylaxis) with penicillin and cannot take oral medication. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. For a penicillin-allergic patient who cannot take oral medication, cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection is used. Tell: clindamycin is the old answer and has been removed.

Correct. He is penicillin-allergic and cannot take oral medication, so the regimen is cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously or intramuscularly 30-60 minutes before the extraction. His reaction was a mild delayed rash, not anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria, so a cephalosporin is allowed.

Ampicillin is the injectable choice for patients WITHOUT a penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication. He reacted to penicillin, and the allergy row covers penicillin or ampicillin. Tell: the allergy history moves the non-oral choice from ampicillin to cefazolin or ceftriaxone.
ruled out by a stated finding

Azithromycin 500 mg is an oral option for penicillin-allergic patients who can swallow. He cannot take oral medication, so an oral agent is out. Tell: allergic and able to take oral medication points to azithromycin, clarithromycin, cephalexin or doxycycline; allergic and unable points to cefazolin or ceftriaxone.
ruled out by a stated finding

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman has had 2 months of low-grade fevers to 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss. She had a tooth extracted 10 weeks ago. A new apical systolic murmur is heard, and splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nail plates) are seen on two fingers. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Two months of lower fevers (38.4 °C), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss is the indolent course of subacute infective endocarditis, in which fever, malaise and weight loss occur over weeks or months. The new murmur and splinter hemorrhages place the problem on a valve, and the recent extraction is a plausible dental source.

Tuberculosis would not explain a new apical systolic murmur or splinter hemorrhages. Her 2 months of lower fevers, fatigue and weight loss after a tooth extraction, plus the new murmur, fit the indolent course of subacute infective endocarditis. Tell: a new murmur with nail hemorrhages points to the valves, not the lungs.

Polymyalgia rheumatica would not produce a new apical systolic murmur or splinter hemorrhages. Low-grade fever, malaise and weight loss over weeks to months with a new murmur after dental work fits subacute infective endocarditis. Tell: look for a new murmur and embolic nail findings before blaming a rheumatologic cause.

Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness with rapid onset over typically 3-10 days, high fevers and systemic toxicity. She has had 2 months of low-grade fever, fatigue and weight loss, which is the indolent subacute pattern. Tell: a duration of months and modest fevers separate subacute from acute.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 77-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His son asks how serious this organism is. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: A relatively good prognosis belongs to viridans streptococcal endocarditis treated before complications occur, not to Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve is the worst combination, with mortality of about 50%.

Surgery is not a rarity to dismiss: it is indicated for heart failure from valvular dysfunction (the most common indication), infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotics, or abscess. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism, with about 50% mortality in prosthetic valve endocarditis. Tell: this organism on a prosthetic valve is high stakes, not a minor infection.

Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis does not resolve within a week; it is the most lethal organism, with mortality of about 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis. Tell: the son's question is about seriousness, and the accurate answer is that this is the highest-risk organism.
It is the most lethal cause

Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism in infective endocarditis, with mortality of about 30% in people who do not inject drugs, 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis and 5% in people who inject drugs. His prosthetic aortic valve puts him in the highest-mortality group.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: An 8-year-old with endocarditis has a sudden fulminant illness with high spiking fevers, unlike the usual slow course in children. Which organisms does this presentation suggest?
opts: Candida is tied to neonates and infants, where fungal disease follows central venous catheters, hyperalimentation, neonatal intensive care or prematurity. An 8-year-old with fulminant spiking fevers fits Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus instead. Tell: fungi go with the neonatal catheter picture.

Correct. Most children have an indolent course with prolonged low-grade fever, but a fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus. The abrupt, high-fever onset in this 8-year-old is the decisive clue.

Viridans group streptococci are the most common organisms in children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, but they cause the usual indolent course of prolonged low-grade fever and fatigue. This child's sudden fulminant illness is the exception. Tell: indolent means viridans; fulminant means pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are linked to prosthetic material, recent surgery and neonatal catheter-related disease, not to a fulminant spiking presentation. Tell: think coagulase-negative staphylococci when a device or graft is involved; high spiking fevers point to pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve placed 3 years ago has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Staphylococcus aureus infection of a prosthetic valve is treated with combination therapy: an antistaphylococcal drug plus rifampin and gentamicin. Because his strain is methicillin-resistant, that drug is vancomycin (nafcillin or oxacillin would be used only for a susceptible strain).

Nafcillin replaces vancomycin only when the culture shows methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. His strain is methicillin-resistant, so vancomycin stays in the combination with rifampin and gentamicin. Tell: susceptible means nafcillin or oxacillin; resistant means vancomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is an empiric regimen used before the organism is known (subacute presentation, native valve, or prosthetic valve in place more than 1 year). His cultures already show methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve. Tell: a known organism replaces the empiric pair with targeted combination therapy.

Penicillin G plus gentamicin is a viridans streptococcal regimen, not a staphylococcal one. Tell: penicillin G pairs with viridans streptococci, while methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve needs vancomycin, rifampin and gentamicin.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man is on day 6 of antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis. He still has fevers, and today's electrocardiogram shows a new conduction block not present on admission. Which complication best explains the new conduction abnormality?
opts: Correct. Persistent fever on day 6 with a new conduction block suggests a perivalvular abscess, meaning infection that extends beyond the valve leaflets into myocardial tissue. When the abscess extends into the upper ventricular septum, it interrupts the conduction system.

Septic emboli to the lungs would cause lung findings, not a new conduction block on the electrocardiogram. A block appearing during treatment points to a perivalvular abscess extending into the upper ventricular septum. Tell: an electrical change localizes the problem to the septum, not the lungs.

Extension of an abscess into the epicardium causes pericarditis, not a conduction block. Conduction is interrupted when the abscess extends into the upper ventricular septum instead. Tell: epicardium means pericarditis; upper septum means heart block.

Rupture of the chordae tendineae causes a new murmur from valvular damage and can lead to heart failure, but it does not interrupt the conduction system. Tell: a new conduction block points to an abscess extending into the upper ventricular septum, not to a chordal problem.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man has 3 days of fever to 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Which organism is a classic cause of this tempo of infective endocarditis?
opts: Viridans streptococci are listed under subacute endocarditis, from the oral cavity, not under the acute form. His 3-day, 40.0 °C, toxic illness is acute. Tell: a rapid toxic course points to Staphylococcus aureus; a slow course after dental work points to viridans streptococci.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are listed with the subacute organisms (only Staphylococcus lugdunensis sometimes causes acute disease) and are early prosthetic valve organisms. Tell: a classic acute organism is Staphylococcus aureus, not a coagulase-negative species.

The gram-negative coccobacilli of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group are listed under subacute endocarditis, not acute. Tell: HACEK organisms are slow, while Staphylococcus aureus is the classic acute cause.

Correct. Three days of fever to 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), rigors, a new murmur and a toxic appearance are an acute tempo, and the acute organisms are beta-hemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible or methicillin-resistant), sometimes Staphylococcus lugdunensis, and enterococci.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 65-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F). Three blood cultures grow viridans streptococci, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows new partial dehiscence of the prosthesis. How many major Duke criteria does he meet?
opts: Both of his findings are major criteria. Viridans streptococci, a typical organism, in separate blood cultures meet the blood culture criterion, and new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve on echocardiogram meets the endocardial criterion. Tell: count the cultures and the echocardiogram separately.

One major criterion undercounts him. The cultures growing viridans streptococci are one major criterion, and the new partial dehiscence of his prosthesis on echocardiography is a second. Tell: new dehiscence of a prosthetic valve is listed as a positive echocardiogram.

Correct. Viridans streptococci, a typical organism, in separate blood cultures meet the major blood culture criterion, and new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve on transesophageal echocardiogram meets the major endocardial criterion. Two major criteria make endocarditis definite; his fever adds a minor criterion.

There are only two major criteria, positive blood cultures and evidence of endocardial involvement, so three is impossible, and he meets both. Tell: his fever and prosthetic valve are minor criteria (fever and predisposition), not extra major ones.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 47-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic macules) on the soles of both feet. Blood cultures are pending. Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Janeway lesions fall into?
opts: Microbiologic evidence is a positive blood culture that does not meet the major criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection. His cultures are still pending, so nothing microbiologic can be counted yet. Tell: microbiologic criteria come from the laboratory, not from the skin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Janeway lesions, the painless hemorrhagic macules on his soles, are a vascular phenomenon, a minor criterion grouped with major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage and conjunctival hemorrhages. His injection drug use and fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) are separate minor criteria.

Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor, and Janeway lesions are not on that list. Tell: the painful lesion (Osler node) is immunologic, while the painless hemorrhagic macule described here (Janeway lesion) is vascular.

The major endocardial criterion requires a positive echocardiogram (oscillating intracardiac mass, abscess or new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve) or new valvular regurgitation. A skin lesion does not show endocardial involvement. Tell: endocardial evidence is seen in the heart; Janeway lesions are seen on the skin.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man with native valve endocarditis is improving on day 4 of intravenous antibiotics and asks whether he can switch to pills so he can go home sooner. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: Stopping after 6 days would leave bacteria alive in the vegetation; therapy must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture. Tell: endocarditis courses are measured in weeks, not days.
Stop when the fever is gone

Fever resolution does not end therapy. The course is bactericidal, parenteral and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture. Tell: feeling better on day 4 is expected and does not shorten the course.

Correct. Antibiotics for endocarditis should be given parenterally, and therapy must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture, because all bacteria in the vegetation must be killed. On day 4 the course has barely begun, so he stays on intravenous therapy.
Pills work just as well now

The standard is parenteral therapy, so pills are not presented as equivalent. Endocarditis antibiotics should be given parenterally, as intravenous therapy with monitoring, typically for 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture. Tell: improvement on day 4 does not change the route.

set1.q: A 12-year-old had a ventricular septal defect closed with a prosthetic patch 4 months ago and is now scheduled for a dental extraction. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Delaying the extraction is not the recommendation. A child within the first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material is high risk, and the answer is prophylaxis before the dental procedure. Tell: high-risk status changes the antibiotic plan, not the timing of needed dental care.

Antibiotics given afterward miss the purpose of prophylaxis, which is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before the procedure. This child does qualify, because he is within 6 months of a prosthetic patch repair. Tell: prophylaxis is always timed before the extraction, never after.

Correct. The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is a high-risk pediatric condition, and he is only 4 months out from his patch. A dental extraction manipulates gingival and periapical tissue, so a single prophylactic dose is given 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

He is still inside the high-risk window: the first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device. A dental extraction with gingival manipulation is exactly the procedure prophylaxis covers. Tell: 4 months after a prosthetic patch is high risk; well past 6 months with no residual defect would not be.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: A 17-year-old who injects drugs has fever, rigors and a tricuspid valve vegetation. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Candida is a neonatal and infant organism, tied to central venous catheters, hyperalimentation, neonatal intensive care and prematurity. None of those apply to a 17-year-old who injects drugs. Tell: Candida belongs to the catheter-bearing infant, not the adolescent who injects drugs.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are linked to prosthetic material, recent surgery and neonatal catheter-related disease. This adolescent has no device; he injects drugs. Tell: injection drug use in an adolescent points to Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct. Adolescents increasingly resemble adults, including injection drug use-associated Staphylococcus aureus disease. His drug use, fever with rigors and a tricuspid valve vegetation fit that adult-type profile rather than the viridans streptococcal disease of younger children.

Viridans group streptococci are the most common organisms in children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, who have indolent disease. This 17-year-old injects drugs, which shifts the organism toward Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: congenital heart disease in a child means viridans; injection drug use in an adolescent means Staphylococcus aureus.

set1.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs has finished a course of intravenous antibiotics for tricuspid valve endocarditis and is preparing for discharge. He says he wants help to stay safe. Which consultation should be arranged?
opts: Nephrology is not among the listed consultations (infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery, addiction medicine), and his antibiotic course is already finished. His request for help staying safe as a person who injects drugs is harm reduction. Tell: no kidney problem is described in the stem.

Correct. He injects drugs, has just finished treatment for tricuspid valve endocarditis and asks for help to stay safe, which is harm reduction. Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, working alongside infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery in the multidisciplinary team.

Dermatology is not among the consultations listed for endocarditis (infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery, addiction medicine), and the stem describes no skin problem. His need is harm reduction for injection drug use. Tell: his own request, staying safe while using, points to addiction medicine.

Ophthalmology is not among the consultations listed for endocarditis care, which are infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery and addiction medicine. His request to stay safe while injecting drugs is a harm-reduction need. Tell: the patient's ask is about drug use, not the eyes.

set1.q: A 31-year-old man who injects drugs has tricuspid valve endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. He has no penicillin allergy. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. His cultures grow methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and he has no penicillin allergy, so he is treated with nafcillin or oxacillin, or cefazolin. Susceptibility is the decisive clue, because vancomycin or daptomycin is the regimen for methicillin-resistant strains.

Vancomycin or daptomycin is the regimen for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. His isolate is susceptible and he has no penicillin allergy, so nafcillin or oxacillin is used. Tell: resistant means vancomycin or daptomycin; susceptible means nafcillin, oxacillin or cefazolin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Penicillin G with gentamicin is a viridans streptococcal regimen, not therapy for Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: penicillin G pairs with viridans streptococci, while a susceptible Staphylococcus aureus gets nafcillin or oxacillin.

Ceftriaxone with azithromycin is not a listed endocarditis regimen: ceftriaxone appears in streptococcal and empiric regimens, and azithromycin is not among the treatment drugs. Tell: methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is treated with nafcillin or oxacillin.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis has 2 days of worsening breathlessness and orthopnea (breathlessness when lying flat). A new, loud regurgitant murmur is heard and crackles fill both lung bases. Which mechanism explains her heart failure?
opts: Myocarditis from fever is not the cause given for heart failure in endocarditis. Congestive heart failure is due to valvular dysfunction, and her new, loud regurgitant murmur shows a failing valve. Tell: a new regurgitant murmur with heart failure points to the valve.

Fluid overload from antibiotics is not the mechanism; congestive heart failure in endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction. Her new, loud regurgitant murmur shows the valve damage driving it. Tell: the murmur links her breathlessness to the infected valve.

Pericardial constriction is not the mechanism. In endocarditis the pericardium is involved only if an abscess extends into the epicardium, causing pericarditis, while heart failure is due to valvular dysfunction. Tell: a new regurgitant murmur means the valve has failed.

Correct. Congestive heart failure in infective endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction. Her new, loud regurgitant murmur reflects valvular damage or rupture of the chordae tendineae, and the resulting regurgitation explains her breathlessness, orthopnea and crackles at both lung bases.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve is having a tooth extracted tomorrow. He has no drug allergies and takes pills without difficulty. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. He has no allergy and can take pills, so oral amoxicillin is the standard. Tell: clindamycin is never the answer in the current regimen.

Prophylaxis is indicated. Prosthetic cardiac valves are on the list of qualifying conditions, and an extraction is a dental procedure that manipulates the gums or roots of the teeth. Tell: no prophylaxis fits procedures like dental radiographs or orthodontic adjustments, not an extraction.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. His prosthetic aortic valve is on the list of conditions for which prophylaxis is reasonable, and a tooth extraction manipulates the gums and roots of the teeth. With no allergy and no trouble swallowing, the regimen is a single dose of oral amoxicillin 2 g 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

Prophylaxis is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before the procedure, not a week of antibiotics afterward. The drug is right, but the timing and duration are wrong. Tell: a correct prophylactic regimen is one dose, given before.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman in urgent care has a fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages (dark lines under the nail plates). Before transfer, a colleague proposes giving a dose of ceftriaxone right away. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Her fever, new murmur and splinter hemorrhages raise suspicion for endocarditis, and empiric therapy is started ONLY after blood cultures have been drawn, three sets from separate sites. Giving ceftriaxone first would compromise the cultures needed to identify the organism and direct the prolonged bactericidal course.

Drawing cultures is required, not avoided: three sets of blood cultures from separate sites, and if the presentation suggests acute disease, 2 cultures within the first 1-2 hours. They must come before any antibiotic. Tell: cultures first is exactly the rule the proposed ceftriaxone dose would break.

Admission is appropriate, not something to avoid. Endocarditis is managed with intravenous antibiotics, hospital admission, close monitoring of labs, renal function and cardiovascular status, and a multidisciplinary team. Tell: transfer and admission are correct; only the pre-culture antibiotic is wrong.

Echocardiography should not be avoided. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, defines the extent of disease and detects vegetations on valve leaflets, so it is a core part of her workup. Tell: the step to avoid here is the premature antibiotic, not imaging.

set1.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has 4 days of fever to 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), rigors and a cough. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, and he looks toxic. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pneumonia would not explain a new holosystolic murmur in a person who injects drugs; fever, rigors, cough and that murmur point to tricuspid valve endocarditis.
A mitral murmur is loudest at the apex rather than the left lower sternal border, and the valve named for people who inject drugs is the tricuspid.
Pericarditis brings positional chest pain and a friction rub, not a new holosystolic murmur with rigors in a person who injects drugs.

Correct. In a person who injects drugs, fever, rigors and a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border point to tricuspid valve endocarditis, the valve named for this group (Staphylococcus aureus causes 80-90% of their tricuspid infections); the lung, a listed embolic site, explains the cough.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 46-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless macules) on his palms. A transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve. Blood cultures are still pending. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Pending cultures do not prevent classification. He already has one major criterion (an oscillating mass on echocardiogram) and three minor criteria (injection drug use, fever of 39.0 °C, Janeway lesions), which is definite. Tell: classify with what you have, since cultures can only add criteria.

Correct. The oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve is a major criterion (positive echocardiogram), and he has three minor criteria: predisposition (injection drug use), fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and Janeway lesions as a vascular phenomenon. One major plus three minor criteria make endocarditis definite.

Possible is one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. He has one major plus three minor criteria, which reaches definite. Tell: count every minor item; injection drug use, fever and Janeway lesions make three.

An oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve is a major criterion, and with three minor criteria it establishes endocarditis rather than excluding it. Tell: pending cultures never rule out endocarditis; they can only add criteria.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 39-year-old woman who injects drugs has native valve endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Ampicillin with gentamicin is not among the staphylococcal regimens. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is treated with vancomycin or daptomycin; gentamicin is an add-on in prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection or for viridans streptococci. Tell: a resistant staphylococcus on a native valve means vancomycin or daptomycin.

Correct. Her cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on a native valve, which is treated with vancomycin or daptomycin. Methicillin resistance is the decisive clue: it rules out nafcillin, oxacillin and cefazolin, which are used for susceptible strains. Therapy is bactericidal, parenteral and prolonged.

Nafcillin or oxacillin treats methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Her isolate is methicillin-resistant, so these drugs will not work. Tell: the word resistant on the culture report moves you from nafcillin or oxacillin to vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Cefazolin is an option for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, alongside nafcillin or oxacillin. Her organism is methicillin-resistant, so cefazolin alone is inadequate. Tell: cefazolin pairs with susceptible strains; resistant strains need vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with a history of infective endocarditis has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), Janeway lesions (painless macules) on her soles and Osler nodes (painful nodules) on two finger pads. One of three blood cultures grows viridans streptococci, the other two are negative, and echocardiography is not yet available. How is her case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: A missing echocardiogram does not block classification. She already has five minor criteria, which alone make endocarditis definite. Tell: definite can be reached by two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor criteria, so no major criterion is required.

Correct. She has five minor criteria: predisposition (previous endocarditis), fever of 38.8 °C, a vascular phenomenon (Janeway lesions), an immunologic phenomenon (Osler nodes) and microbiologic evidence (one positive culture of three, which misses the major criterion). Five minor criteria make endocarditis definite.

Possible is one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. She has five minor criteria, which reaches definite without any major criterion. Tell: count all five, which are prior endocarditis, fever, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes and the single positive culture.

Five minor criteria confirm endocarditis rather than exclude it. The single positive culture for viridans streptococci misses the major criterion but still counts as minor microbiologic evidence. Tell: one positive culture of a typical organism is not dismissed like a contaminant.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 52-year-old woman on long-term immunosuppression has endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Candida. Which complication is most likely?
opts: Correct. Her blood cultures grow Candida, which makes this fungal endocarditis, and the most likely complication of fungal endocarditis is embolism with occlusion of larger peripheral arteries. Her immunosuppression is the setting, but the organism is what predicts the complication.

Nothing about fungal endocarditis suggests a quick cure; its expected course is complicated by embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries. Tell: Candida on culture signals an embolizing, hard-to-treat infection, unlike viridans streptococci, which carry a relatively good prognosis when treated early.

Rheumatic carditis is not listed as a complication of endocarditis, fungal or otherwise. With Candida on culture, the complication to expect is embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries. Tell: a fungal organism points to large-vessel emboli, not to a separate inflammatory carditis.

A pericardial knock is not among the complications of fungal endocarditis. The fungal complication to anticipate is embolization that occludes larger peripheral arteries. Tell: the danger with Candida is a large-vessel arterial occlusion, a vascular event, not an added heart sound.

set2.q: A 41-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for tricuspid valve endocarditis. On day 2 he develops a new cough, and chest imaging shows several new scattered lesions in both lungs. Which complication best explains these findings?
opts: Nothing in the stem describes vomiting, and aspiration would not explain several scattered lesions in both lungs. The lung is a listed embolic site of endocarditis, and his tricuspid vegetation is the source. Tell: multiple bilateral lesions in someone with a right-sided vegetation point to emboli.

Correct. He has tricuspid valve endocarditis, a right-sided vegetation, and on day 2 develops a new cough with several scattered lesions in both lungs. The lung is a listed embolic complication of infective endocarditis, along with the spleen, kidney and liver, and multiple new lesions fit septic emboli.

Drug-induced lung injury is not a listed complication of endocarditis, and new scattered lesions on day 2 fit embolization better. The lung is one of the listed embolic sites, with the spleen, kidney and liver. Tell: a tricuspid vegetation plus multiple new lung lesions spells septic emboli.

Congestive heart failure is a recognized cardiac complication of endocarditis, but it would not produce several discrete new lesions scattered through both lungs. Tell: multiple separate lesions point to emboli from the tricuspid vegetation; heart failure reflects valvular dysfunction, not seeding.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with acute endocarditis asks why the team is so worried when she felt well a week ago. Which statement about untreated acute endocarditis is accurate?
opts: It can be fatal within weeks

Correct. She felt well a week ago, the rapid onset typical of acute disease (typically 3-10 days, with high fevers and systemic toxicity). A virulent organism rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites, and if untreated, acute endocarditis progresses to death within weeks.

Acute endocarditis does not resolve on its own; if untreated, it progresses to death within weeks. Tell: a virulent, invasive organism that rapidly damages the heart and seeds extracardiac sites demands treatment, and spontaneous resolution is not part of either form.

Smoldering harmlessly is wrong on both counts. Even subacute endocarditis is gradually progressive over weeks or months, and acute disease rapidly damages cardiac structures. Tell: she was well a week ago, the rapid acute pattern that kills within weeks if untreated.
It is mainly a lung infection

Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness that rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites; the lung is only one of several embolic targets, along with the spleen, kidney and liver. Tell: the infection sits on the endocardium and spreads outward, so it is a heart infection, not mainly a lung one.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, a transesophageal echocardiogram shows no vegetation, and he has no predisposing heart condition, no drug use and no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Correct. He meets one major criterion, a typical organism (Staphylococcus aureus) in two separate blood cultures, and one minor criterion, fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). The negative transesophageal echocardiogram and absent predisposition, vascular and immunologic findings add nothing, so one major plus one minor is possible endocarditis.

Definite needs two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor. He has only one major (the cultures) and one minor (fever), because the echocardiogram is negative and he has no predisposition, vascular or immunologic findings. Tell: a second major criterion is missing.

Nothing here rules endocarditis out: two separate blood cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus meet a major criterion, and his fever is a minor criterion. One major plus one minor makes endocarditis possible. Tell: a clean echocardiogram removes one major criterion, not the diagnosis.

Criteria are met. Staphylococcus aureus is a typical organism, so two separate positive cultures meet the major blood culture criterion, and a fever of 38.9 °C is above the 38.0 °C minor threshold. Tell: count the cultures first, because two separate positives of a typical organism are a major criterion.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis brings an old wallet card that lists clindamycin for her dental prophylaxis. She has a penicillin allergy. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. Her previous endocarditis still qualifies her, so with a penicillin allergy she receives azithromycin or clarithromycin, doxycycline, or cephalexin if her reaction was not anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, so her old card is out of date. Tell: a penicillin-allergic patient now receives azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline or, without a severe reaction history, cephalexin.

Amoxicillin is a penicillin, and she has a penicillin allergy, so it is not an option. Penicillin-allergic patients who can take oral medication receive azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline or cephalexin. Tell: the fix for an outdated clindamycin card is a non-penicillin alternative.
ruled out by a stated finding

She still needs prophylaxis, because previous infective endocarditis is on the list of qualifying conditions. Tell: what changed is the drug on her card, not her need for prophylaxis before dental work that manipulates the gums or roots or perforates the oral mucosa.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman with native mitral valve endocarditis after dental work has blood cultures growing penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. Which antibiotic is a directed choice?
opts: Daptomycin is listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, alongside vancomycin, not as a streptococcal choice. Her cultures grow penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. Tell: viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin.

Correct. Her cultures grow penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci after dental work, and viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin, or vancomycin. Adding gentamicin allows a 2-week regimen only for uncomplicated disease with rapid response and no chronic kidney disease.

Nafcillin and oxacillin treat methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and her organism is viridans streptococci. Tell: antistaphylococcal penicillins follow a staphylococcal culture, while streptococci get penicillin G or ceftriaxone.

Rifampin and gentamicin are add-ons in staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, combined with vancomycin or nafcillin; they are not a backbone for streptococci. Tell: the viridans streptococcal backbone is penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with gentamicin only as an optional partner.

set2.q: A 9-year-old with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Prophylaxis is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before the procedure, not afterward. This child qualifies: unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease plus a tonsillectomy that incises respiratory mucosa. Tell: a dose given afterward is not prophylaxis.

Canceling is not the recommendation. A high-risk child undergoing an invasive respiratory procedure receives prophylaxis beforehand and proceeds with surgery. Tell: high-risk heart disease changes the antibiotic plan, not whether the tonsillectomy happens.

Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, including palliative shunts and conduits, is a high-risk pediatric condition, and tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision. Both conditions are met, so prophylaxis is given as a single dose 30-60 minutes before surgery.

Both the child and the procedure qualify. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is a high-risk pediatric condition, and a tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision. Tell: prophylaxis requires a high-risk condition AND a qualifying procedure, and both are present here.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 61-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) and Osler nodes (painful red nodules on the pads of her fingers). Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Osler nodes fall into?
opts: Predisposition is a separate minor criterion covering predisposing heart conditions or injection drug use. In her case the prosthetic mitral valve fills that slot, not the Osler nodes. Tell: predisposition describes the patient's background; Osler nodes are a finding on exam.

The major blood culture criterion requires a typical organism in two separate blood cultures or persistently positive cultures, so a skin finding cannot fill it, and no cultures are reported here. Tell: Osler nodes are seen at the bedside and count only as a minor immunologic criterion.

Correct. Osler nodes are an immunologic phenomenon in the modified Duke criteria, a minor criterion shared with glomerulonephritis, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. Her other findings count separately: the prosthetic valve is predisposition, and 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) meets the fever criterion of 38.0 °C or higher.

Vascular phenomena are embolic findings: major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions. Osler nodes are not on that list. Tell: painful Osler nodes are immunologic; painless Janeway lesions are vascular.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman has subacute endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Eikenella corrodens, a member of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Rifampin is an add-on in staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, combined with nafcillin or vancomycin plus gentamicin. It is not a treatment for HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms. Tell: there is no prosthetic valve and no staphylococcus here, so rifampin has no role.

Correct. Her cultures grow Eikenella corrodens, a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism, and HACEK endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily for 4 weeks. The listed alternative is ampicillin-sulbactam for 4 weeks.

Nafcillin is a staphylococcal drug, used for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus on native or prosthetic valves. It is not a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) regimen. Tell: nafcillin follows a staphylococcal culture; Eikenella calls for ceftriaxone.

Vancomycin is not a listed regimen for HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms; it appears in streptococcal, enterococcal and staphylococcal regimens. Eikenella corrodens endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone or ampicillin-sulbactam. Tell: a HACEK organism on culture means ceftriaxone.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 73-year-old man who lives at home has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and a new murmur. He has had no recent hospital stay, procedure or urinary symptoms, and no primary source of infection is found. Two separate blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. How do these cultures count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Blood cultures count on their own. Echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement is a separate major criterion, not a prerequisite for the culture criterion. Tell: each major criterion stands independently, and these cultures already meet one.

Correct. Community-acquired enterococci in the absence of a primary focus count as a typical organism for endocarditis. He lives at home, has had no hospital stay, procedure or urinary source, and two separate cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis, so the major blood culture criterion is met.

A positive culture counts as the minor microbiologic criterion only when it does not meet the major criterion. Community-acquired enterococci without a primary focus are a typical organism, so two separate positive cultures meet the major criterion. Tell: typical organism plus two separate cultures equals major.

Only single positive cultures of coagulase-negative staphylococci or diphtheroids, or of organisms that rarely cause endocarditis, are excluded as contaminants. Enterococcus faecalis in two separate cultures is a typical organism. Tell: two separate cultures of a typical organism are never dismissed.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 59-year-old man with native aortic valve endocarditis and a large vegetation asks whether a blood thinner would prevent a stroke. He has no other reason for anticoagulation. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Anticoagulation is not beneficial in patients with native valve infection; it is only controversial in patients with prosthetic valves. He has native aortic valve endocarditis and no other reason for anticoagulation, so heparin or warfarin should not be started to prevent a stroke.

Appropriate antibiotic therapy is the expected treatment and should continue; surgery is considered only when infection is not resolving with it. The choice to avoid is anticoagulation, which is not beneficial in native valve endocarditis such as his. Tell: stopping effective therapy is never the safe answer.

Monitoring renal function is not a choice to avoid, and nothing in the stem argues against checking his kidneys while infectious disease directs therapy and monitoring. The choice to avoid is anticoagulation, which is not beneficial in native valve infection. Tell: only one option lacks benefit here.

Consulting infectious disease is appropriate: infectious disease manages antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring pending disposition. The choice to avoid is anticoagulation, which is not beneficial with native valve infection. Tell: consultations help; the blood thinner does not.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 62-year-old man with fever has four sets of blood cultures drawn. One set grows coagulase-negative staphylococci, and the other three are negative. How should this single positive culture be counted under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Correct. A single positive culture for coagulase-negative staphylococci, with the other three sets negative, is excluded from the criteria because coagulase-negative staphylococci (like diphtheroids) are common culture contaminants. It counts as neither a major criterion nor the minor microbiologic criterion.
As the major blood culture criterion

The major blood culture criterion needs a typical organism, such as viridans streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus, in two separate cultures, or persistently positive cultures. One of four sets growing coagulase-negative staphylococci meets neither. Tell: one positive set out of four is not persistent bacteremia.

Vascular phenomena are embolic findings such as major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions. A culture result is never counted there. Tell: vascular criteria are found on exam or imaging; cultures fall under the blood culture or microbiologic criteria.

One positive culture is not definite proof: a single coagulase-negative staphylococcal set is excluded as a common contaminant, and even one major criterion alone does not make endocarditis definite. Definite endocarditis requires two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor. Tell: a lone contaminant set counts toward no criterion.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with a prosthetic aortic valve is scheduled for a screening colonoscopy and has no active infection. She asks whether she needs antibiotics beforehand. Which advice is most accurate?
opts: Amoxicillin 30-60 minutes before is the standard regimen for qualifying dental procedures, not for colonoscopy. Gastrointestinal procedures such as colonoscopy do not require prophylaxis. Tell: her prosthetic valve matters only when the procedure itself qualifies.
Prophylaxis is a single dose before a qualifying procedure, never a 7-day course, and colonoscopy does not require any prophylaxis. Tell: gastrointestinal procedures are on the no-prophylaxis list.

Intravenous vancomycin is not among the prophylaxis regimens, and colonoscopy does not require prophylaxis anyway. Tell: gastrointestinal and genitourinary procedures need no antibiotic, whatever the agent.

Correct. Gastrointestinal and genitourinary procedures, including colonoscopy, upper endoscopy and cystoscopy, do not require endocarditis prophylaxis. Her prosthetic aortic valve does not change this, because the procedure itself does not qualify and she has no active infection.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: An 83-year-old woman is ready for discharge on day 9 of a planned 6-week course of intravenous antibiotics for endocarditis. She is deconditioned and cannot yet walk safely on her own. Which part of the multidisciplinary plan addresses this?
opts: Deconditioning is not an indication for surgery. The indications are heart failure due to valvular dysfunction, infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotics, abscess and fungal infection. Tell: her problem is mobility, which is a disposition and rehabilitation question.

Stopping antibiotics on day 9 of a planned 6-week course does nothing for her mobility and leaves her infection undertreated; infectious disease continues antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring. Tell: rehabilitation addresses walking, and the antibiotics continue.

Correct. The multidisciplinary team plans disposition, and rehabilitation is part of that plan for a deconditioned 83-year-old who cannot walk safely. Infectious disease continues to oversee the remaining weeks of antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring.

Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; nothing in her history suggests drug use, and it does not address deconditioning. Tell: her need is mobility, which is met through rehabilitation in disposition planning.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 44-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) and Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages) on fundoscopy, meeting three minor Duke criteria. He has received no antibiotics. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure him that it is not endocarditis

Three minor criteria do not exclude endocarditis; they leave the diagnosis open, and blood cultures from separate sites come next, before any antibiotic. Tell: an open diagnosis calls for testing, not reassurance.
Order a chest radiograph and discharge

A chest radiograph is not among the listed tests and cannot show vegetations, and discharge would abandon an open workup. He needs three sets of blood cultures from separate sites and transesophageal echocardiography. Tell: the workup is cultures and echocardiography, not a chest film.
Draw blood cultures from separate sites

Correct. With three minor criteria (injection drug use, fever of 38.8 °C and Roth spots) and no antibiotics given, the next step is three sets of blood cultures from separate sites, before empiric therapy. A typical organism in the cultures would add a major criterion, and one major plus three minor criteria is definite.
Start oral amoxicillin and recheck later

Starting oral amoxicillin before cultures breaks the rule that empiric therapy starts only after blood cultures are drawn, and oral therapy does not meet the parenteral standard. Tell: cultures first, then parenteral antibiotics.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and malaise that began a week after a dental extraction. A new murmur of mitral regurgitation is heard. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn. Which organism are they most likely to grow?
opts: Enterococci are a subacute cause, but they come from the genitourinary tract. His illness began after a dental extraction, an oral source. Tell: a urinary source means enterococci; a mouth source means viridans streptococci.

Candida is listed as the fungal cause of endocarditis, separate from the bacterial causes of subacute disease. A smoldering illness that began a week after a tooth extraction points to the oral cavity, the source of viridans streptococci. Tell: a dental source means viridans streptococci, not a fungus.

Correct. Three weeks of low-grade fever and malaise is a subacute course, and its onset a week after a dental extraction points to the oral cavity, the source of viridans streptococci. Viridans streptococci are a classic subacute organism and a leading cause of native valve endocarditis.

Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism and a leading acute cause, with a rapid, toxic course. Three weeks of low-grade fever and malaise after a dental extraction is subacute disease from an oral source. Tell: dental work plus an indolent course points to viridans streptococci, not a skin organism.

set2.q: A 64-year-old man will finish 5 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for endocarditis after discharge. Which consultant manages his antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring?
opts: Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; it does not manage antibiotic therapy or monitoring. Tell: the outpatient antibiotic plan belongs to infectious disease.

Dermatology is not among the listed consultations (infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery, addiction medicine) and has no role in managing endocarditis antibiotics. Tell: the outpatient antibiotic plan belongs to infectious disease.

Correct. Infectious disease is consulted for antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring pending disposition, so it oversees his remaining 5 weeks of intravenous antibiotics after discharge. Cardiothoracic surgery and addiction medicine have separate roles in the multidisciplinary team.

Cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for surgery and anticoagulation, not the outpatient antibiotic plan. Tell: the surgeon decides about operating, while infectious disease runs the antibiotics and monitoring.

set2.q: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has 5 days of high fever and rigors. Transthoracic imaging shows a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve, and three sets of blood cultures are drawn from separate sites. Which organism are the cultures most likely to grow?
opts: Viridans streptococci come from the oral cavity and lead community-acquired native valve disease. Her exposure is injection through the skin, and Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism. Tell: injection drug use plus a tricuspid vegetation means Staphylococcus aureus, not an oral streptococcus.

Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract, and nothing here suggests a urinary source. Tricuspid endocarditis in a person who injects drugs is Staphylococcus aureus in 80-90% of cases. Tell: injection drug use points to a skin organism, not a urinary one.

Candida is a fungal cause and not the organism of injection drug use; in people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all endocarditis. Tell: a tricuspid vegetation in a person who injects drugs points to Staphylococcus aureus in 80-90% of cases.

Correct. In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus, a skin organism, causes more than 60% of all endocarditis and 80-90% of cases in which the tricuspid valve is infected. Her 5 days of high fever and rigors with a large tricuspid vegetation fit that pattern.

set2.q: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody test has a new murmur. She has no fever, repeated blood cultures are negative, and echocardiography shows small sterile-appearing valve vegetations. Which is the most likely cause of her valve lesion?
opts: Subacute infective endocarditis would be expected to bring fever and positive cultures; she has neither, and her lupus features point to a non-infective valve lesion. Tell: malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody with sterile-appearing vegetations mean Libman-Sacks, not infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

Acute infective endocarditis would bring fever and positive cultures; she has no fever, repeatedly negative cultures and sterile-appearing vegetations, so she meets neither the fever nor the culture criterion. Tell: lupus features with sterile vegetations point to Libman-Sacks, a non-infective mimic.
ruled out by a stated finding

Device endocarditis requires an implanted cardiac device, and none is described. Her lupus features, absent fever and negative cultures point to non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis. Tell: with no device in the history, device endocarditis cannot be the answer.

Correct. She has features of systemic lupus erythematosus (malar rash, painful joints, positive antinuclear antibody), and lupus may present with non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis. No fever, repeatedly negative blood cultures and sterile-appearing vegetations fit this autoimmune mimic rather than infection.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve is booked for a diagnostic bronchoscopy. No biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Which advice about endocarditis prophylaxis is most accurate?
opts: Not every bronchoscopy qualifies. Bronchoscopy is on the list of procedures that do not require endocarditis prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the mucosa, such as a biopsy, and none is planned here. Tell: his prosthetic valve does not change this, because the procedure itself does not qualify.

Prophylaxis is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before a qualifying procedure, never a week-long course. And this bronchoscopy does not qualify, because no biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Tell: a week of antibiotics is a treatment pattern, not prophylaxis.

Intravenous vancomycin is not one of the prophylaxis regimens, which use amoxicillin, ampicillin, cephalosporins, macrolides or doxycycline, and this procedure needs no prophylaxis at all. Diagnostic bronchoscopy without biopsy or mucosal incision is on the no-prophylaxis list. Tell: no incision means no drug.
None is needed for this procedure

Correct. Bronchoscopy does not require endocarditis prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as a biopsy. His is diagnostic with no biopsy or incision planned, so no antibiotic is given despite the prosthetic mitral valve; respiratory prophylaxis is reserved for procedures that incise or biopsy mucosa.

set2.q: An 85-year-old man with degenerative aortic valve disease presents with fever and a new murmur. His family is surprised that a heart infection could occur at his age. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Age raises the risk rather than lowering it: risk is increased among the elderly, and people over 60 account for more than 50% of cases. Tell: his age and his degenerative valve disease both increase risk.
Over-60s are over half of cases

Correct. Risk is increased among the elderly, and people over 60 account for more than 50% of cases, although endocarditis can occur at any age. His degenerative aortic valve disease is now one of the leading predisposing conditions in high-income countries.
It occurs mainly in drug users

Injection drug use is one listed risk factor, but endocarditis does not occur mainly in people who use drugs; people over 60 account for more than 50% of cases. Tell: in high-income countries, degenerative valve disease and devices lead the predisposing conditions.

Endocarditis does not occur mainly in children; people over 60 account for more than 50% of cases. Tell: his age and degenerative valve disease place him squarely in the most common group, the elderly.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with subacute endocarditis has a fundoscopic examination that shows Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages). What process causes these spots?
opts: Optic nerve swelling is not what Roth spots are; they are white-centered retinal hemorrhages. The cause is vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. Tell: Roth spots are hemorrhages in the retina, not swelling of the optic nerve.

Hypertensive retinal change is not the mechanism of Roth spots. In endocarditis, Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages caused by vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. Tell: a white-centered retinal hemorrhage in a patient with endocarditis is a Roth spot from small-vessel vasculitis.

Correct. Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages produced by vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. In this man with subacute endocarditis they are the eye finding of the disease, alongside exam findings such as splinter hemorrhages, petechiae, Osler nodes and Janeway lesions.

No trauma or detachment is part of this picture; he has subacute endocarditis with no injury described. Roth spots arise from vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. Tell: in endocarditis, think vasculitis for white-centered retinal hemorrhages.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a fever, a new murmur and Janeway lesions (painless macules on her soles), and two blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Her transesophageal echocardiogram is read as normal. Which conclusion is correct?
opts: She has a skin infection instead

Her Janeway lesions, new murmur, fever and two cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus point to endocarditis, not a skin infection, and a normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule endocarditis out. Tell: the whole picture, not one negative test, decides.

Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, but a normal study does not necessarily rule out endocarditis. Her fever, new murmur, Janeway lesions and two blood cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus keep the diagnosis open, so workup and treatment continue.

A normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis, even though the test is highly sensitive and specific. Tell: with Staphylococcus aureus in two cultures, a new murmur and Janeway lesions, a single normal image cannot exclude the diagnosis.

Two separate blood cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus are not explained away as contamination; with fever, a new murmur and Janeway lesions they support endocarditis. Tell: the normal echocardiogram is the result that fails to settle the question, not the cultures.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has been in the hospital for 9 days after hip surgery. She develops a new fever, and two sets of blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus; she has no indwelling catheter, and examination finds no wound or other source. Which diagnosis must be suspected?
opts: Dismissing both culture sets as contamination ignores the key rule: health care-associated endocarditis should be suspected in a hospitalized patient who develops fever with positive blood cultures and no apparent source. Tell: two concordant sets plus new fever in an inpatient demand an endocarditis workup.
ruled out by a stated finding

Postoperative atelectasis would not produce positive blood cultures. A hospitalized patient with new fever and positive cultures without an apparent source is exactly when health care-associated endocarditis should be suspected. Tell: bacteremia without a source in an inpatient points to the endocardium, not the lungs.

Drug fever would not produce positive blood cultures. A new fever with two culture sets growing Staphylococcus aureus and no apparent source in a hospitalized patient raises health care-associated endocarditis. Tell: positive cultures make this an infection, not a drug reaction.

Correct. She has been in the hospital for 9 days and now has fever with two sets of positive blood cultures and no apparent source (no catheter, no wound). Health care-associated endocarditis is less common but should be suspected in exactly this situation, and 25-35% of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated.

set2.q: A 7-year-old with congenital heart disease is admitted with viridans streptococcal endocarditis. Which approach to antibiotic therapy is most appropriate?
opts: This gets two details wrong for a child. Parenteral therapy in pediatric endocarditis means intravenous, not intramuscular, and the dose is weight-based rather than a fixed adult dose. Tell: a 7-year-old receives intravenous drug dosed by weight, so both intramuscular and fixed adult dosing are traps.

A short oral course does not meet the standard. Pediatric antibiotics for endocarditis must be prolonged, bactericidal and parenteral, given intravenously and dosed by weight, the same as in adults. Tell: both oral and one week contradict the prolonged intravenous rule.

Observation leaves a confirmed viridans streptococcal infection untreated. Pediatric management is essentially the same as adult management: prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral, pathogen-directed and weight-based antibiotics. Tell: every listed pediatric strategy starts with antibiotics; none is watchful waiting.

Correct. Management in children is essentially the same as in adults: antibiotics that are prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral (intravenous, not intramuscular), pathogen-directed and weight-based. This 7-year-old's dose is calculated by weight, given intravenously and continued for a prolonged course.

set2.q: A 69-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter for 2 days of new confusion. She has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). Brain imaging shows multiple small scattered lesions without a large stroke. Which mechanism best explains her confusion?
opts: No conduction block is described, and low-flow ischemia would not explain fever, a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae. Multiple small scattered lesions fit septic emboli from a vegetation. Tell: petechiae are an embolic phenomenon, linking the brain lesions to the same embolic process.

No sedating drug is described, and sedation would not produce multiple small scattered brain lesions. Her fever, new murmur and conjunctival petechiae point to emboli from a vegetation reaching the brain. Tell: lesions on imaging make this structural, not a drug effect.

Correct. Fever, a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae suggest endocarditis, and multiple small scattered brain lesions fit septic emboli. Cerebral complications include ischemic stroke, abscess, intracranial hemorrhage and meningitis, and neurologic deficits are a recognized manifestation of endocarditis.

Meningitis is one listed cerebral complication of endocarditis, but it would not account for multiple small scattered lesions on brain imaging. Her new murmur and conjunctival petechiae point to emboli showering from a vegetation. Tell: scattered focal lesions mean emboli, not a primary meningeal infection.
