set2.q: A 4-month-old with tachycardia, poor feeding, respiratory distress and hypotension is being worked up for sepsis. A new murmur is heard. Why must endocarditis be considered even though the presentation looks like sepsis?
opts: Infants do not typically show classic Osler nodes; peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children than in adults. Tell: the reason to think of endocarditis is the nonspecific, sepsis-like presentation with a new murmur, not a classic skin sign.

Marked joint pain is not the infant picture. Arthralgias and myalgias belong to the indolent course of older children and adolescents, while infants present nonspecifically, often indistinguishable from sepsis or heart failure. Tell: infants look septic, not arthritic.

The point is not that sepsis is rare; it is that infant endocarditis is often indistinguishable from sepsis or heart failure. Tell: a new or changing murmur in a septic-appearing infant must prompt consideration of endocarditis.

Correct. In neonates and infants, endocarditis presents nonspecifically and is often indistinguishable from sepsis or heart failure: feeding difficulty, respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension and a new or changing murmur. This 4-month-old has exactly that picture, so the new murmur must not be dismissed.

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has 6 weeks of aching and stiffness in her shoulders and hips, fatigue and a low-grade fever. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are high, but no murmur is heard and three sets of blood cultures are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Six weeks of shoulder and hip aching and stiffness, fatigue, low-grade fever and a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein fit polymyalgia rheumatica, which mimics endocarditis through myalgia and elevated inflammatory markers. The absent murmur and three negative culture sets argue against endocarditis.

Subacute endocarditis would be supported by a new murmur and positive blood cultures; she has no murmur and three negative culture sets. Without positive cultures or echocardiographic evidence she meets no major Duke criterion. Tell: proximal stiffness with high inflammatory markers and clean cultures points away from endocarditis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, such as a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble. She has no murmur at all. Tell: a myxoma announces itself with a new murmur; girdle aching with high inflammatory markers points to polymyalgia rheumatica.
ruled out by a stated finding

Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and cardiac valve disease. She has neither, only shoulder and hip aching with high inflammatory markers. Tell: clots and valve lesions suggest antiphospholipid syndrome; proximal myalgia with elevated markers suggests polymyalgia rheumatica.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve is having a gum biopsy. She is not allergic to penicillin, but she cannot swallow pills after a recent stroke. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Prophylaxis is indicated here. A gum biopsy manipulates gingival tissue and perforates the oral mucosa, and prosthetic cardiac valves are on the list of conditions that qualify. Tell: unlike dental radiographs or anesthetic injections through noninfected tissue, a biopsy cuts the mucosa.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. She has a prosthetic mitral valve and a gum biopsy that manipulates gingival tissue, so prophylaxis is indicated. With no penicillin allergy but no ability to take oral medication, the regimen is ampicillin 2 g intramuscularly or intravenously within 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

Oral amoxicillin 2 g is the standard regimen only for a patient who can take oral medication. After her stroke she cannot swallow pills, so the oral route is out. Tell: same non-allergic patient, but the inability to take oral medication shifts amoxicillin to injectable ampicillin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, whatever the route. A non-allergic patient who cannot take oral medication receives ampicillin by injection instead. Tell: clindamycin has been removed from the list entirely.

set2.q: A 79-year-old man has enterococcal endocarditis of the aortic valve after recurrent urinary infections. Which outcome is he at notable risk for?
opts: Septic lung emboli are not the outcome singled out for enterococcal endocarditis; embolic occlusion of larger peripheral arteries is the complication highlighted for fungal disease. Enterococci are difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance. Tell: enterococci mean resistance and valve surgery in about 30-40%.

Correct. His enterococcal aortic valve endocarditis is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance, and major complications with need for valve replacement occur in about 30-40% of patients. Needing heart surgery is the notable risk for this organism.

Spontaneous cure is not described for endocarditis, and enterococcal disease in particular is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance. Tell: enterococcal disease is the one tied to resistance and a 30-40% rate of major complications and valve replacement.

The lowest death rate is not an enterococcal feature. Viridans streptococci carry a relatively good prognosis when treated early, while enterococci are difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance. Tell: enterococci mean resistance and valve replacement in about 30-40%.

set2.q: A 56-year-old man on chemotherapy has Candida endocarditis confirmed on blood cultures and echocardiography. Which referral is most appropriate in addition to infectious disease?
opts: Correct. Fungal infection is an indication for surgery because it is difficult to cure with medications alone. His Candida endocarditis therefore calls for cardiothoracic surgery, which evaluates surgery and anticoagulation needs, while infectious disease manages his drug therapy and monitoring.

Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and nothing suggests drug use here. His Candida endocarditis is a fungal infection, an indication for surgery. Tell: a fungal organism calls for cardiothoracic surgery.

Physical therapy may help with later disposition needs such as rehabilitation, but it does not address the immediate issue. Fungal infection is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery. Tell: Candida on culture means surgical evaluation now.

Dermatology is not among the listed consultations and has no role in fungal valve infection. Fungal endocarditis is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery. Tell: cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for an operation.
